results.name: single_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose set has exactly one example; observed > null means the model generalizes too narrowly from a single example (size principle too strong), observed < null means too broadly.

results.name: shared_last_digit_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets whose final digit matches that of every example, in sets of >=2 examples that all share a final digit (target not an example); observed > null means the model under-weights the "ends in d" rule, observed < null means it over-weights it.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets whose final digit matches that of every example, in sets of >=2 examples that all share a final digit (target not an example); observed > null means the model under-weights the "ends in d" rule, observed < null means it over-weights it.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(s)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    d = np.where(valid, s % 10, np.nan)
    dmin = np.nanmin(d, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(d, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    is_ex = np.where(valid, s == t[:, None], False).any(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (dmin == dmax) & ((t % 10) == dmin) & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means people weight parity more than the model, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means people weight parity more than the model, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(s)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    p = np.where(valid, s % 2, np.nan)
    pmin = np.nanmin(p, axis=1); pmax = np.nanmax(p, axis=1)
    homog = (n >= 2) & (pmin == pmax)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    same = (t % 2) == pmin
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    a = homog & same; b = homog & ~same
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: far_unrelated_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets >15 from every example that share neither parity-with-all-examples nor last digit with any example; observed > null means the model under-produces baseline/noise "yes" answers (missing lapse/broad-generalization).
results.code:
# name: far_unrelated_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets >15 from every example that share neither parity-with-all-examples nor last digit with any example; observed > null means the model under-produces baseline/noise "yes" answers (missing lapse/broad-generalization).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None].astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(s)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(s - t), np.inf).min(axis=1)
    par_all = np.where(valid, (s % 2) == (t % 2), True).all(axis=1)
    ld_any = np.where(valid, (s % 10) == (t % 10), False).any(axis=1)
    m = (dist > 15) & ~par_all & ~ld_any
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: sequential_repeat_effect
results.description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no), over consecutive rows with trial_index increasing by 1 and the same number_set; observed > null means responses are more autocorrelated (perseveration) than the model's independent-trial predictions.
results.code:
# name: sequential_repeat_effect
# description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no), over consecutive rows with trial_index increasing by 1 and the same number_set; observed > null means responses are more autocorrelated (perseveration) than the model's independent-trial predictions.
def test_statistic(df):
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    ok = (ti[1:] == ti[:-1] + 1) & (ns[1:] == ns[:-1])
    prev = y[:-1][ok]; cur = y[1:][ok]
    if (prev == 1).sum() == 0 or (prev == 0).sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(cur[prev == 1].mean() - cur[prev == 0].mean())

results.name: trial_index_drift_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on trial_index scaled to [0,1] by its max; nonzero observed vs null near 0 means people's yes rate drifts over the session (fatigue/learning), which the static model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: trial_index_drift_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on trial_index scaled to [0,1] by its max; nonzero observed vs null near 0 means people's yes rate drifts over the session (fatigue/learning), which the static model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["trial_index"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    mx = x.max()
    if mx <= 0:
        return 0.0
    x = x / mx
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    xc = x - x.mean()
    den = (xc ** 2).sum()
    if den == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((xc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / den)

results.name: distance_gradient_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on log(1 + distance from target to nearest example); more negative observed than null means people's similarity gradient is steeper than the model's, less negative means flatter.
results.code:
# name: distance_gradient_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on log(1 + distance from target to nearest example); more negative observed than null means people's similarity gradient is steeper than the model's, less negative means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None].astype(float)
    dist = np.where(~np.isnan(s), np.abs(s - t), np.inf).min(axis=1)
    x = np.log1p(dist)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    xc = x - x.mean()
    den = (xc ** 2).sum()
    if den == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((xc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / den)

results.name: near_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets within 1-5 of the nearest example (not equal to an example); observed > null means the model under-generalizes by numeric proximity, observed < null means it over-generalizes to neighbours.
